AerialYield-T¹M: A Greenhouse Tomato Dataset with Six-Stage Ripeness Masks, Fruit Counts, and Baseline Validation

Abstract

Tomato harvest and grading decisions in protected cultivation depend on visual ripeness judgements made across whole trusses rather than on isolated fruit, and the commercial reference for that judgement is the six-stage colour classification used for red-fleshed cultivars. We present AerialYield-T¹M, a curated real-image resource of 535 RGB images of greenhouse tomato plants, annotated with 9,260 per-fruit polygon instances across the six USDA/Silal ripeness stages: green, breakers, turning, pink, light red and red. The release provides class-specific binary masks, an overall fruit mask, single-channel semantic label maps, image-level fruit counts, COCO and YOLO exports, SHA-256 hashes, source metadata and a leakage-safe, group-aware train/validation/test split. AerialYield is the broader project name and does not imply that every image is aerial; this release contains no harvested weight, fruit mass or plot-level yield measurement, and the count labels should be interpreted as image-level fruit counts rather than yield estimates. We additionally report held-out baseline validation for the three tasks this release is built to support — ripeness classification, semantic segmentation and image-level counting — trained and evaluated on the recommended split.

Confirmed release facts: 535 real RGB images; 9,260 annotated tomato instances; 6 ripeness classes; 380/79/76 train/validation/test images (block-grouped, leakage-safe). Baseline results: classification macro-F1 = 0.452 (accuracy 0.819); segmentation foreground mIoU = 0.407 (Dice 0.515, pixel accuracy 0.980); counting MAE = 5.02 fruit (RMSE 9.53, R² 0.541) — all on held-out test images.

Background & Summary

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is among the most intensively cultivated horticultural crops in protected environments, and harvest timing is governed almost entirely by visual maturity. The commercial reference framework is the colour-based classification used by USDA graders for red-fleshed cultivars, which partitions fruit into green, breakers, turning, pink, light red and red on the basis of the proportion of the surface that has departed from green. This scheme is deliberately perceptual — defined by what a grader sees — which makes it directly transferable to image-based systems but also sensitive to illumination, viewing angle and partial visibility. Automating the judgement therefore requires image collections in which the ripeness attribute is attached to individual fruit rather than to whole images, with the surrounding canopy clutter preserved rather than removed.

Selective robotic harvesting requires a perception stack that can localise a fruit, decide whether it has reached the target maturity class, and do so under occlusion by leaves, stems and neighbouring fruit. Greenhouse monitoring and yield forecasting require repeatable counts of fruit at each maturity stage. Both tasks degrade sharply when fruit are small, heavily occluded, or embedded in foliage of similar hue — precisely the regime in which green and breaker-stage tomatoes appear. Public tomato resources with dense, per-fruit ripeness masks anchored to a published grading standard remain limited, which motivates a focused release built the same way as its sibling greenhouse fruit dataset, AerialYield-B²D.

Our contribution is AerialYield-T¹M, a focused greenhouse tomato dataset with six-stage ripeness masks and image-level count metadata. T¹M denotes the current single-source release; AerialYield refers to the broader research project and is not a claim that every image is aerial or that yield measurements are included. The release record, counts, metadata and technical-validation results reported here refer to the 535 real RGB images that constitute the current data acquisition.

Methods

Image acquisition

The current release contains 535 RGB images of greenhouse tomato plants, at 7680×4320 pixels (363 images, landscape) or 4320×7680 pixels (172 images, portrait). No embedded EXIF metadata is present in the source JPEG files; acquisition date and time are therefore recovered from the filename pattern written by the capture pipeline and retained in the release manifest as filename-derived rather than embedded metadata — the same distinction the sibling blueberry release draws for its video-derived frame subset. Recovered filenames place all 535 images on a single acquisition date across three capture sessions, with 211, 152 and 172 images respectively; within a session the embedded frame index advances in near-constant steps, consistent with frame extraction from continuous video. Capture device, sensor model and flight/handling parameters are recorded in the release manifest where available and are otherwise marked for confirmation with the acquisition team.

Data collection workflow

Data collection was treated as a scene-level sampling task rather than a class-balanced object-capture task. Images were collected from greenhouse tomato plants while keeping fruit trusses in their natural canopy context, including occlusion, foliage, lighting variation and mixed ripeness stages. The resulting class imbalance reflects the crop state captured during acquisition rather than an artificial balancing target.

  1. Step 1 — Identify greenhouse tomato scenes containing visible fruit trusses, including mixed-ripeness scenes and natural occlusion.
  2. Step 2 — Acquire RGB frames, retaining source JPEG files and filename-derived acquisition metadata.
  3. Step 3 — Preserve greenhouse context rather than isolating individual fruit, so downstream users can evaluate segmentation and detection under realistic cluster, foliage and lighting conditions.
  4. Step 4 — Annotate individual tomatoes with polygon boundaries and assign the ripeness attribute for each annotated fruit, over the visible extent only for occluded or border-intersecting fruit.
  5. Step 5 — Export class-specific and overall masks, apply orientation handling, threshold mask conversion, and semantic-map generation.
  6. Step 6 — Generate image-level counts, source metadata, SHA-256 hashes, a leakage-safe fixed split, quality reports and baseline-validation artifacts for release.

Ripeness taxonomy

Labels follow the six-stage USDA colour classification for red-fleshed tomato cultivars, applied by visual inspection rather than laboratory maturity determination. Class names, label identifiers and mask colours are defined in class_map.json and used consistently across semantic maps, binary masks, overlay figures and the count tables below.

Annotation products

Annotations are instance-aware: each visible tomato is traced with a polygon and assigned a ripeness attribute, over its visible extent only. Class-specific and overall binary masks, semantic label maps, COCO/YOLO detection exports, per-instance ripeness labels and image-level counts are all derived from this polygon annotation, so that boxes, masks and counts describe the same underlying instance set rather than being produced independently.

Preprocessing pipeline

  1. Scan raw RGB image, mask and annotation folders.
  2. Rasterise per-class binary masks from the source annotation, thresholded at intensity >127 where sourced from lossy exports, and preserve the class-agnostic overall mask.
  3. Composite per-class masks into a single-channel semantic label map (IDs 1–6), writing 255 wherever more than one class mask claims a pixel.
  4. Extract per-instance crops and detection boxes directly from the polygon annotation's own bounding box — not from mask connected components. On this release, per-class mask images are a lossy export whose compression artefacts can split one fruit's silhouette into more than one connected blob; the polygon annotation, not that derived mask geometry, is treated as the instance ground truth. Mask connected-component counts are still computed and reported (Table 4) as a mask-quality signal.
  5. Compute SHA-256 hashes for every released image, and image-quality metrics (brightness, saturation, Laplacian sharpness) on downsampled copies.
  6. Construct leakage-safe grouping keys and generate the deterministic train/validation/test split (see below).
  7. Train and evaluate baseline classification, segmentation and counting models on the recommended split, and write metadata tables, figures and audit reports.

Recommended dataset split

Because the 535 images are extracted video frames rather than independent photographs, images a few frames apart within the same capture session can be near-duplicate views of the same fruit; splitting them across train/validation/test would leak information and inflate held-out performance. Each of the three capture sessions is therefore first divided into fixed-width frame-number blocks, and whole blocks — never individual frames within a block, and never a block split across subsets — are assigned to train, validation or test with a stratified, seeded assignment targeting a 70/15/15 image ratio and approximate per-class instance balance. This block-grouped strategy resolves 535 images into 56 leakage-control groups, compared with only 3 groups if whole sessions were used as the unit (too coarse for a 70/15/15 split) or 535 if individual frames were used (which is what produces the leakage this strategy avoids). Checked against the realised split, 0 of the 56 blocks are split across subsets, and only 3.9% of temporally-adjacent frame pairs (21 of 532) cross a split boundary — the residual is the unavoidable boundary between two adjacent blocks assigned to different subsets, not a failure of the grouping itself.

Ethics statement

The dataset contains plant and crop images. It does not contain human participants, human-derived data or animal subjects.

Data Records

The prepared release comprises 9,260 crop image files, per-class and overall binary masks, semantic label maps, COCO/YOLO detection exports, and metadata/split/report tables for all 535 source images, totalling 10,913 derived files (≈1.2 GB) built from a 4,287-file (≈4.6 GB) raw source archive.

FolderContents
images/RGB JPEG source images (535 files).
masks_binary/<class_name>/Lossless per-class binary masks, one folder per ripeness class.
masks_semantic/Single-channel semantic label maps, values 0–6 and 255 for ignore pixels.
masks_overall/Class-agnostic fruit masks.
classification/crops/<class_name>/9,260 per-instance classification crops.
detection/{coco,yolo}/Per-split COCO JSON and YOLO-format detection exports.
metadata/Image manifest, instance table, classification-crop manifest, class map.
splits/Train, validation and test file lists.
reports/, figures/Preprocessing audit, validation reports and figures.

Technical Validation

Completeness and file integrity

Every one of the 535 RGB images has a complete set of six class-specific masks and one overall mask; no missing or orphaned artefacts were found. All 535 SHA-256 image hashes are unique and all filenames are unique.

Image geometry and orientation

Images contain no embedded EXIF orientation tag; 363 are 7680×4320 (landscape) and 172 are 4320×7680 (portrait). No image–mask dimension mismatches were found.

Mask conversion and overlap audit

Class-overlap pixels (two class masks claiming the same pixel) occur in 5 of 535 images, 13,930 pixels in total — negligible against the ≈9.5 billion analysed pixels. Class-union-versus-overall-mask disagreement occurs in 297 of 535 images, with a median magnitude of 13 pixels against a ≈33.2-million-pixel image (maximum 9,592 pixels). Overlap pixels are encoded as 255 in the semantic maps and are excluded from segmentation loss.

Qualitative overlay inspection

Representative images were reviewed with their masks and ground-truth boxes rendered as an overlay (Figures 3–4) to check RGB–mask alignment, the plausibility of assigned ripeness labels, and the handling of dense trusses, partial occlusion and mixed maturity within a single truss.

Image-quality screening

Brightness, saturation and Laplacian sharpness were measured on downsampled copies of all 535 images to screen for gross acquisition failures. Mean brightness was 111.2 (σ 9.1), mean saturation 109.9 (σ 17.8), and mean Laplacian sharpness variance 750.9 (σ 292.4); the distributions (Figure 7) support the absence of grossly blank or unusable images.

Ripeness classification baseline

Classification — the primary recommended task for this release — was validated with a ConvNeXtV2-Tiny backbone (27.9M parameters), class-balanced via a weighted training sampler and a class-weighted loss, trained on the crop-level training split with the label-smoothed cross-entropy objective and evaluated on the held-out test crops. Training used AdamW with a cosine learning-rate schedule and early stopping on validation macro-F1.

Semantic segmentation baseline

Segmentation was validated with an FPN-style decoder over a ConvNeXtV2-Tiny encoder (28.6M parameters) — the same architecture family used for the sibling blueberry release's baseline — trained on full images resized to 512×512 and evaluated on the held-out test split.

Usage Notes

For semantic segmentation, use the RGB images as inputs and the semantic label maps as targets, treating value 255 as an ignore label so class-overlap pixels do not contribute to the loss. For multilabel or class-agnostic segmentation, use the per-class or overall binary masks. For object detection or instance-level crop experiments, use the COCO/YOLO exports; instances are defined by the polygon annotation, not by mask connected components, because touching fruit and lossy mask compression can both distort component boundaries. For counting, use the image-level count fields directly rather than deriving counts from connected components. For ripeness classification, use the per-instance crops and the class attribute.

The size of this release should be assessed by annotation density as well as image count: 535 images contain 9,260 annotated fruit instances. Breakers (127) and red (121) remain rare relative to green (6,558) and light red (1,409) — a genuine property of the sampled truss population, not an artefact — so class imbalance should be treated as part of the benchmark. The classification and segmentation baselines above show this directly: both tasks perform well on the well-represented classes and substantially worse on breakers and red, and per-class metrics on those classes should be reported alongside their supporting instance counts rather than in isolation.

The recommended split is block-grouped by acquisition session and frame proximity rather than by whole image, for the reasons given under "Recommended dataset split" above. Users defining alternative splits on this release should preserve that grouping constraint; naive image-level random splitting of frame-extracted data of this kind will produce optimistic held-out results.
